posts.title: Check your cmux sessions from Android
posts.promise: Muxer links an Android app to cmux terminals through a relay on your computer.
posts.whatItIs: Muxer is an open source relay and Android app for viewing and controlling cmux terminal sessions over a private network. A beginner could test a narrow setup guide or onboarding aid as a separate project; that adaptation is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers who use cmux and want to check sessions from a phone might pay for setup help or a simpler companion. The source gives no customer or payment evidence.
loop: Install the relay on a Mac with cmux.
Put the relay behind HTTPS access limited to your own devices.
Pair the Android app using a one-time code.
Review sessions and notifications on the phone.
Revoke a paired device if it is lost.
posts.evidence: The project README describes the relay, Android app, pairing flow, terminal controls, and private-network setup.
posts.uncertainty: This is a documented product description, not independent evidence of customer use. Access setup requires care: the phone can read terminals and type into cmux. A human must manage network exposure and decide which devices to pair.
first24Hours: Read the README security and setup sections.
Write down the steps needed for a private HTTPS setup.
Ask one cmux user to review a hypothetical beginner setup guide.

ease.reason: The README gives concrete setup steps, but a first test needs cmux, Android, and private HTTPS networking.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: cmux users wanting phone access might pay for setup help; the source establishes no buyers or demand.

feasibility.reason: A narrow setup guide is plausible in four weeks; validating the workflow requires access to cmux and Android.

autonomy.reason: Relay streaming and notifications repeat automatically, while device pairing and network access need human oversight.

evidence.reason: The README documents a working relay and app workflow, but offers no cited evidence of real use.

posts.title: A visual home for AI workflows
posts.promise: n8n combines workflows and AI agents with testing, logs, and human approval steps.
posts.whatItIs: n8n describes a platform where users connect workflow steps and AI agent steps, configure tools, test behavior, and publish. A beginner could prototype one bounded workflow in n8n; the workflow choice and intended customers here are hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small team that wants to automate a repeated internal process might pay for workflow setup or support. The source does not establish buyers or demand.
loop: Choose a narrow task with steps you can specify.
Connect its inputs and actions in n8n.
Add an AI step only where judgment is needed.
Set tool limits and human approval points.
Test a run, inspect its steps, and revise before publishing.
posts.evidence: The n8n page describes deterministic workflows, AI agents, testing, execution logs, scheduling, integrations, and human approval controls.
posts.uncertainty: The source is n8n's own product page and does not demonstrate a specific student workflow or customer result. A person must choose safe tools, review model decisions, and approve consequential actions.
first24Hours: Pick one low-risk task you already understand.
Sketch its inputs, steps, and places needing human approval.
Use n8n's test option to inspect a small example workflow.

ease.reason: The page says users can describe an agent or build by hand and test it, though choosing integrations takes learning.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: a small team may pay for workflow setup; the product page does not establish demand or customer spending.

feasibility.reason: A single bounded workflow is a plausible four-week experiment given templates and test runs; task-specific fit is unproven.

autonomy.reason: Published workflows can schedule and handle errors, while tool limits and human approval steps still need deliberate setup.

evidence.reason: The product page documents workflow and agent features, but its claims are first-party and no specific live demo is attached.

posts.title: Ask a quick question, then clear the chat
posts.promise: Howler puts a model-powered question and answer in a temporary macOS window.
posts.whatItIs: Howler is a macOS menu bar app that sends questions to a model service the user configures, streams answers, and clears the conversation when closed. A beginner might explore a separate ephemeral note-taking tool; that adaptation is hypothetical.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: Mac users who want transient AI answers might pay for a privacy-focused utility. The attached README does not establish customer demand or sales.
loop: Configure a model service and store its API key in Keychain.
Open the letter and type a question.
Optionally attach pasted text, an image, or a screen capture.
Review the streamed answer and ask a follow-up.
Close the letter to clear the conversation from memory.
posts.evidence: The README describes the menu bar interface, model configuration, streaming replies, attachments, and that messages live in memory and burn when the letter is closed.
posts.uncertainty: The privacy and product details come from the project's own README, without independent validation. A person must configure a model, protect API credentials, and judge answer accuracy; attached content goes to the configured service.
first24Hours: Read the README's setup and privacy sections.
Try the documented demo mode without a key or network.
List what remains stored and what is sent to the configured model.

ease.reason: The README offers a demo mode without a key or network, while normal use requires macOS and model setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: some Mac users may pay for transient AI answers; the README provides no evidence of buyers or revenue.

feasibility.reason: A narrow demo is accessible, but building a comparable macOS app involves Swift and model-service setup.

autonomy.reason: Answer streaming and conversation clearing are automatic, but users configure services and review answers themselves.

evidence.reason: The first-party README documents a detailed product workflow and demo mode, without independent real-use evidence.
